Hi Oliver / Lena  

quick technical answers ahead of Wednesday: 

1) Vector dims (128 vs 256)
- Tradeoffs: 256-d vectors often improve recall for high-entropy text and can help downstream re-rankers, but they double storage and per-op compute. If your current 128-d quality meets your SLAs, we recommend staying at 128 for now and validating with an A/B on a sample corpus. If you see precision/recall gaps on long-tail queries, consider 256 for the reranker inputs only.

2) Normalization strategy
- Store normalized vectors if your retrieval stack expects cosine/dot-product on normalized vectors

This saves query-time CPU and keeps similarity semantics stable. Caveat: storing normalized vectors reduces ability to switch to similarity metrics that rely on magnitude (rare). Our migration plan supports both: we can accept raw vectors and normalize in our ingest pipeline, or accept normalized vectors and treat them as-is. For migration from VectorOne we'll provide a normalization pass that verifies length & re-normalizes if needed.

3) Batching & server-side continuous batching
- Benefits: our serving runtime implements continuous batching which groups in-flight small requests into larger GPU-friendly batches, improving throughput and p95 latency under moderate load. This removes need for client-side large batches and simplifies client code. For your QPS (80 avg, 220 peak) we recommend enabling server-side batching with a 32-token per-batch target and a max latency budget of 30ms. That yields better unit economics and lower p95 compared to client batching at 16.

4) Migration approach from VectorOne
- We typically run a side-by-side migration: export vectors -> run normalization & dimension validation -> ingest into a shadow index on Redwood -> run comparison evaluations (recall/rr@10) before cutover. We'll provide an ingestion script and a small ETL job template.

5) SDK & Auth
- For hosted API: API keys with scoped credentials and rotation are common. For private deploys we support mTLS and customer-managed keys via KMS. We'll bring a short SDK example to the deep dive (Node + Python). Example minimal request (Node):

// pseudo-code example
const Redwood = require('@redwood/inference-sdk');
const client = new Redwood.Client({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY });
const res = await client.embeddings.create({
  model: 'redwood-embed-001',
  input: ['doc1 text', 'doc2 text'],
});

Happy to dig into performance numbers Wed. I attached a short migration checklist.
